name: Markdown
seoDesc: Markdown: work out markdown percent from the actual selling price. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Markdown calculator returns markdown percent from the field on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. It suits a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Markdown calculator work?
sections.html:
The Markdown calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports markdown percent in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the actual selling price.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html: • A measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.

sections.title: What are the variables at a glance?
sections.html:
Everything the page asks for and everything it reports, side by side. The roles matter: a value you supply is read from the form, a calculated value is derived from the others and cannot be set directly.

sections.title: The formula behind the Markdown calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Markdown percent=markdown ÷ actual selling price
Markdown percent=(-actual selling price + original selling price) ÷ actual selling price
Markdown=-actual selling price + original selling price

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Actual selling price = 10 and Markdown = 10. The calculator returns Original selling price = 20 and Markdown percent = 100 %.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Original selling price = 20 and Markdown percent = 100 % should be roughly the size you expected from Actual selling price = 10 and Markdown = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in percent, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.
  • Shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • %, opening in percent

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Markdown calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the actual selling price — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Markdown calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Markdown calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns markdown percent, derived from the actual selling price. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Markdown calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the actual selling price, which is a single field. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter original selling price in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Original selling price opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Original selling price = 20. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Markdown calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
